title: Why I Built The Oversight Report
author: Robert Benard, MS, RN, CNS, AGACNP-BC, PMHNP-BC
excerpt: Families kept asking me if a nursing home was any good. I never had a good answer. The data existed — it was just impossible to find. So I built a tool that puts it all in one place.
content:
Before this was a website, it was a question I kept getting asked and could never answer well.

I have spent most of the last twenty years working in ICUs, emergency departments, psych emergencies, and addiction medicine. Across all of those settings, there is one version of the same conversation that comes up over and over. A family member pulls you aside — in the hallway, in the waiting room, sometimes on the phone — and asks some version of: is this nursing home any good?

Maybe their parent just got admitted somewhere and they are not sure about it. Maybe they are trying to decide between two facilities for a discharge. Maybe something happened and they are wondering whether it was the facility or just bad luck. The question is always some version of the same thing: how do I know if this place is okay?

And for years, I never had a good answer.

Not because the information did not exist. It did. CMS — the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services — collects an enormous amount of data on every Medicare-certified nursing home in the country. Inspection results. Complaint investigations. Penalties. Staffing levels reported quarterly by each facility. Ownership records. Quality measures. Cost reports. Eighteen different federal data sources covering 14,713 facilities.

The problem was that none of it was usable for a normal person. The data sits in different government systems, in different formats, on different update schedules. It comes as zipped CSV files with cryptic column names. There is no single place where a family can look up a facility and see what the federal government actually knows about it — not in a way that makes sense at two in the morning when you are trying to make a decision.

The gap was not data. It was access.

I kept thinking someone would build this. A tool that just pulls together what CMS already collects and makes it searchable in plain language. Not a rating site with ads. Not a placement service that gets paid by facilities when a patient moves in. Just the public data, organized so you can actually read it.

Nobody did. So I built it.

What it is

The Oversight Report covers all 14,713 Medicare-certified skilled nursing facilities in the United States. For each one, you can see inspection citations, complaint investigations, civil money penalties, staffing data from the Payroll-Based Journal, ownership and chain relationships, quality measures, and cost report disclosures — all on one page.

The first version was built across about thirty hours on February 23 and 24, 2026. The goal was simple: take the 18 CMS data sources, connect them by facility, and make one readable page per nursing home. That is what launched. It was not polished. It was honest. It showed what the data actually said.

Who it is for

Families who need to evaluate a nursing home and want to see what the federal record shows. Attorneys building elder abuse or negligent care cases who need inspection and staffing history they can cite. Journalists investigating ownership patterns or enforcement trends. Advocates and ombudsmen tracking a facility or chain over time.

It is not built for facility administrators — there are compliance products that sell to the industry. It is not a referral service — those have financial relationships with the facilities they recommend. This serves the other side: the people trying to figure out whether a place is safe.

The short version

Families kept asking me if a place was any good. The data to answer that question existed, but it was scattered across 18 federal databases and impossible for a non-expert to use. I wanted to make it easy. That is what this is.

— Robert Benard, MS, RN, CNS, AGACNP-BC, PMHNP-BC
Founder, DataLink Clinical LLC
February 24, 2026
